blocks.text: Suppose point charges q₁, q₂, q₃, ………, qₙ are arbitrarily distributed within an arbitrarily shaped closed surface, as shown in Fig. 9.14. Since φₑ = q/ε₀, so the electric flux passing through the closed surface is:

blocks.alt: An irregular pink closed surface containing seven small orange point charges labelled q1, q2, q3, q4, q5, q6 and qn.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.14 (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.14).

blocks.text_alt: φₑ = (1/ε₀) × (Total charge enclosed by closed surface)

blocks.text: where Q = q₁ + q₂ + q₃ + ………… + qₙ, is the total charge enclosed by closed surface. Equation 9.14 is mathematical expression of Gauss's law which can be stated as:

blocks.title: Gauss's law
blocks.text: The total electric flux through any closed surface is 1/ε₀ times the total charge enclosed in it.

Gauss's law can be applied to calculate the electric intensity due to different charge configurations. In all such cases, an imaginary closed surface is considered which passes through the point at which the electric intensity is to be evaluated. This closed surface is known as Gaussian surface. Its choice is such that the flux through it can be easily evaluated.
As an example, let us find the electric field at any point outside a sphere on which a charge q is placed.
The Field of a Charged Conducting Sphere

Consider a conducting sphere of radius R containing a charge q. We know that all the charge is distributed uniformly over the surface of sphere as shown in Fig. 9.15. We can also conclude from the spherical symmetry that the electric field is radial everywhere and that its magnitude depends only on the distance r from the centre of the sphere. Thus, the magnitude E is uniform over a spherical surface with any radius r concentric with the spherical conductor. Therefore, we take our Gaussian surface as an imaginary sphere with radius r greater than the radius R of the conducting sphere.
The area of the Gaussian sphere is 4πr², and because E is uniform over the sphere, the total flux through the whole surface will be:

blocks.alt: An inner circle (the conducting sphere, radius R, marked in cyan) with + charges on its surface, and a larger concentric circle (the Gaussian sphere, radius r). Magenta field lines run radially outward beyond both circles, dashed inside the conductor.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.15 (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.15).

blocks.text: This shows that the field at any point outside the sphere is the same as though the entire charge were concentrated at its centre. Just outside of the sphere, where r = R, i.e.,

blocks.latex: \text{In vector form:} \qquad \vec{E} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,\frac{q}{R^2}\,\hat{r} \qquad \text{where } \hat{r} \text{ is the direction of } \vec{E}.
blocks.text_alt: In vector form:   E = (1/4πε₀)(q/R²) r̂   where r̂ is the direction of E.
